This ordinance specifically states that American rules of evidence are not to be applied by the judges. Hearsay and double hearsay evidence is permitted, and it is left entirely to the discretion of the judges whether or not the defense be permitted to question the authenticity or probative value of evidence...

In contrast to the defence the prosecution was able to obtain anything they thought necessary from anywhere in the world. They could provide documentary proof of numerous details and cross-connections about which the defence generally had no inkling, since, contrary to what one might have supposed from the statements of [U.S. officers] Storey and Coogan, the defence was generally allowed access only to incriminating material. Defence counsel had no opportunity to make their own selection of exonerating material.

Such rules of hearsay led to nonsense that not even "mainstream" historians believe anymore:

Ilse Koch on trial at Dachau for making human lamp shades at Buchenwald Her lampshades were actually made of goat skin. (!)

(The "human lampshade" story was the accusation that several prisoners at the Buchenwald camp were killed and had their skin made into lampshades. The civilians of nearby towns were paraded into a showcase of atrocity porn including lampshades, shrunken heads and rumors of a bear pit into which prisoners would be thrown.

It's funny how no historian has been prosecuted for doubting any of those things, despite the fact that it is impossible to define a law against Holocaust denial that won't catch "acceptable" revisionism. Is it criminal for me to say that only 10,999,999 people were killed in the Holocaust? Is it criminal for the Auschwitz museum to have lowered its claimed death count from 4M to 1M?)

There are a lot of reasons to doubt the Holocaust and they're certainly not exclusive to stories and accusations that the majority of people and historians doesn't believe anymore. However, that is for a different post.

This gets extremely problematic and potentially disastrous if you consider how many convictions rely on those extrajudicial proceedings initiated against the original alleged murders:

a precedent set in 2011, when former Ohio autoworker John Demjanjuk became the first person to be convicted in Germany solely for serving as a camp guard, with no evidence of involvement in a specific killing.

(Demjanjuk actually died during appeal, so he's not actually considered to have been convicted)

Of course there will never be a chance for these people to have even the slightest chance at having their cases reexamined on the grounds that the original conclusions of the Nuremberg trials were improperly conducted and therefore should be estranged. It is especially difficult to question the Nuremberg trials in court because doing so is illegal in many countries including Germany.
